title: Episode 23: The Great Camel Experiment and the Ghost of Hi Jolly
description:
In 1856, Secretary of War Jefferson Davis launched one of the most eccentric military experiments in American history: importing seventy-five camels from Egypt and Turkey to blaze wagon routes across the arid deserts of Arizona. Led by a charismatic Syrian-Greek handler named Hi Jolly, the US Camel Corps proved remarkably effective, but the Civil War abandoned the beasts to roam the southwest as wild desert legends.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Following the Mexican-American War and the California Gold Rush, the United States faced an enormous geographical challenge: thousands of miles of scorched, trackless desert separating the settled East from the Pacific Coast. Traditional army mules and horses were dropping dead of thirst, heat exhaustion, and starvation along the arid trails of northern Arizona. In eighteen fifty-five, an ambitious Secretary of War proposed an outrageous, radical solution: import dozens of live camels from the Middle East to form a specialized military caravan in the American Southwest. What followed was a hilarious, bizarre, and astonishingly successful military trial, guided by a spirited Ottoman camel driver named Hi Jolly, that culminated in wild feral beasts roaming the Arizona badlands for half a century. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: JEFFERSON DAVIS AND THE DESERT SHIP
In the early eighteen fifties, the United States Army was confronted with the brutal logistics of Manifest Destiny. The newly acquired territories of New Mexico, Arizona, and California were separated from the rest of the nation by the Great American Desert—a vast expanse of scorching sand, rugged volcanic rock, and alkaline water holes that swallowed supply wagons and killed livestock by the thousands. Army horses and mules required twenty gallons of fresh water a day and tons of grain, making long-distance military patrols almost impossible. Enter Jefferson Davis, then serving as United States Secretary of War under President Franklin Pierce. A visionary when it came to military modernization, Davis had spent years studying European colonial campaigns in North Africa. He became convinced that the only creature capable of conquering the Southwestern deserts was the camel—the ancient 'ship of the desert.' In eighteen fifty-five, Davis persuaded a skeptical Congress to pass a special appropriation bill granting thirty thousand dollars for 'the purchase and importation of camels and dromedaries to be employed for military purposes.' In May of that year, the Navy storeship USS Supply, commanded by Lieutenant David Dixon Porter, set sail across the Atlantic on a bizarre shopping expedition to Tunis, Malta, Smyrna, and Alexandria. Davis personally briefed Porter before departure, emphasizing that camels had sustained the Roman legions and Ottoman armies across the most punishing arid wastelands of the ancient world, and arguing that the young American Republic must embrace the same ancient wisdom to connect its eastern capitals with the Pacific shore.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE VOYAGE OF THE USS SUPPLY
Converting a wooden sailing ship into a floating camel barn proved to be a comical naval adventure. Lieutenant Porter designed custom deck stalls lined with heavy canvas slings to keep the heavy beasts upright during rough Atlantic swells, along with specialized ventilation hatches. In Middle Eastern ports, Porter and Army Major Henry Wayne haggled with Ottoman traders and Egyptian pashas, acquiring thirty-three prime camels, including one-humped Arabian dromedaries for speed and massive two-humped Bactrian camels for heavy freight. Crucially, the expedition also hired several experienced native handlers to teach American soldiers how to pack, ride, and care for the exotic creatures. Among these foreign handlers was a gregarious twenty-eight-year-old Syrian-born Ottoman subject named Philip Tedro—a man of mixed Greek and Syrian ancestry who had recently completed the Islamic pilgrimage to Mecca and was known by his Arabic title, Hadji Ali. American soldiers, completely incapable of pronouncing his Arabic name, immediately nicknamed him 'Hi Jolly.' In February eighteen fifty-six, the USS Supply sailed into the Gulf of Mexico, weathering ferocious hurricanes before unloading thirty-four healthy camels—including one born at sea—at the port of Indianola, Texas, to the utter bewilderment of local cowboys.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE BEALE EXPEDITION ACROSS ARIZONA
The true operational test of the U.S. Camel Corps came in the summer of eighteen fifty-seven, when Lieutenant Edward Fitzgerald Beale was commissioned to survey a new four-thousand-mile wagon road along the thirty-fifth parallel from Fort Defiance, New Mexico, across the trackless northern Arizona desert to the Colorado River. Beale departed with twenty-five camels, heavily laden with military supplies, marching alongside standard army mules and horses. At first, American soldiers cursed the animals: the camels smelled pungent, spat sticky cud when irritated, and let out terrifying, guttural groans whenever they were loaded with baggage. Furthermore, army horses and mules panicked at the sight and scent of the humped monsters, stampeding through camps and throwing their riders. But as the expedition pushed into the waterless, lava-strewn wilderness of northern Arizona, Beale's skepticism transformed into utter awe. While army mules collapsed from dehydration and refused to eat the prickly desert vegetation, the camels thrived. They devoured bitter greasewood, thorny mesquite, and sharp prickly pear cactus with relish. They walked thirty miles a day over razor-sharp volcanic malpais rock without needing shoes, carrying eight hundred pounds of cargo each, and went up to ten days without drinking a single drop of water. When Beale reached the Colorado River near present-day Needles, California, the camels plunged into the wide, rushing river and swam across effortlessly, proving their absolute superiority over mules.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CIVIL WAR ABANDONS THE CORPS
Despite the undeniable triumph of Beale's expedition, the U.S. Camel Corps was doomed by national politics. In eighteen sixty-one, the American Civil War erupted. Jefferson Davis became the President of the Confederate States of America, and anything associated with his pre-war initiatives was viewed with deep suspicion and hostility by Northern politicians in Washington. With the nation consumed by catastrophic warfare in Virginia and Tennessee, military funding for desert transportation evaporated overnight. The camels stationed at Camp Verde in Texas were captured by Confederate troops, who had no idea how to manage them and eventually neglected or traded them away. Meanwhile, in California and Arizona, Union quartermasters auctioned off their camel herds to private packing companies, circuses, and mining operators. Unable to train stubborn American mule skinners to pack camels properly, many private owners simply turned the beasts loose into the Arizona wilderness to fend for themselves. For decades afterward, small breeding herds of wild camels wandered freely across the Sonoran desert, grazing along the Gila River and surprising startled prospectors and Apache hunters who could scarcely believe their eyes.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE LEGEND OF THE RED GHOST
The abandonment of the Camel Corps gave rise to one of the most chilling urban legends of the frontier West: the terrifying saga of the Red Ghost. In eighteen eighty-three, near Eagle Creek in eastern Arizona, a terrified ranch woman was trampled to death in her yard by a monstrous, reddish beast with a towering hump. Days later, prospectors reported seeing a giant red camel galloping through the desert canyons—and strapped tightly to its back with rawhide thongs was the desiccated, mummified corpse of a human skeleton, its fleshless skull bobbing with the animal's stride. For a decade, stories of the ghost camel spread across Arizona campfires; ranchers claimed the creature attacked cattle herds, smashed corrals, and vanished into the night like an apparition. In eighteen ninety-three, an Arizona farmer named Mizoo Hastings spotted the reddish camel grazing peacefully in his turnip patch. Hastings raised his rifle and shot the beast dead. Upon examining the fallen animal, locals discovered deep scars where heavy rawhide straps had grown directly into the camel's skin, confirming the horrific truth: years earlier, someone had tied a dead man to the feral camel's pack saddle and turned it loose into the desert, creating an accidental frontier phantom.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: HI JOLLY'S FINAL TRAIL
While the camels faded into frontier legend, their beloved handler Hi Jolly became an indelible Arizona folk hero. Philip Tedro never returned to the Ottoman Empire; he adopted Arizona as his permanent home, married a local woman in Tucson, raised a family, and became a proud American citizen. For decades, Hi Jolly worked as a desert prospector, scout for the U.S. Cavalry during the Apache Wars, and operated a regional courier service between desert mining towns. He was universally beloved throughout the territory for his warmth, generosity, and endless storytelling. Even in his old age, Hi Jolly kept two pet camels at his home in the desert town of Quartzsite, often walking into the desert to search for wild camels he believed were still roaming the hills. When he passed away in nineteen oh-two at the age of seventy-four, the people of Arizona honored him with deep affection. In nineteen thirty-five, the Arizona Highway Department erected a magnificent stone pyramid monument over his grave in Quartzsite, topped with a bronze silhouette of a camel and containing his original ashes and camel bell. Today, thousands of travelers along Interstate ten pause at Quartzsite to pay homage to the Greek-Syrian driver who helped blaze the highways of the American Southwest atop a desert ship.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LIVING SHIPS OF THE WEST
The legacy of Jefferson Davis's U.S. Camel Corps lingered across the desert Southwest long after the military experiment was officially abandoned. For more than half a century, confirmed sightings of feral camels continued to baffle prospectors, Native American hunters, and railroad crews throughout Arizona, Nevada, and northern Mexico. In nineteen oh-one, a wild camel was spotted drinking peacefully from the Gila River near Florence, Arizona; in nineteen thirteen, another solitary beast was recorded grazing near the Mexican border; and as late as nineteen forty-one, a Douglas, Arizona newspaper reported a verified sighting of a feral camel wandering through the rugged badlands of Sonora. The camels had proven with absolute biological finality that the ecology and harsh terrain of the American desert were perfectly suited to their evolutionary strengths. Today, in the small town of Quartzsite, Arizona, Hi Jolly's iconic stone pyramid monument stands as a beloved roadside pilgrimage for thousands of travelers along Interstate ten. Philip Tedro's adventurous life and the strange, humped beasts he guided across uncharted canyons remain an endearing testament to the eccentric, multicultural tapestry that shaped the American frontier.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The Great Camel Experiment of 1856 remains one of the most delightfully eccentric chapters in American military history. It proves that innovation often wears an unusual face, and that the spirit of the American frontier was shaped by wanderers from every corner of the Earth. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we climb the Colorado Rockies to explore a palace built entirely of ice. Until then, stay curious.
